lesson.title: Wearing Someone Else's Address
lesson.summary: A spoofing attack forges the source address on network traffic, an IP address, a MAC address, or another identifier, so it appears to come from somewhere it did not, tricking systems that trust that address into acting on it.
lesson.body:
A great deal of networking infrastructure makes decisions based on trusting an address field: a firewall rule might allow traffic from a specific trusted IP address, a switch forwards frames based on the MAC address in the frame's header, a server might grant access based on where a request claims to originate. Spoofing attacks exploit the fact that these address fields, on their own, are just values written into a packet or frame, and nothing inherently prevents a sender from writing a false one.

IP spoofing means forging the source IP address field in a packet, so the packet appears to come from a different machine than the one that actually sent it. Because IP address checks are used throughout networking, in firewall rules, in access controls, in reputation based filtering, a spoofed source address can let an attacker's traffic slip past checks that would otherwise reject traffic from the attacker's real address. MAC spoofing works at a lower layer: a device changes the MAC address it presents on the local network, which can let it impersonate another device on that same local segment, for instance to intercept traffic intended for the device it's impersonating or to bypass access controls tied to a specific known MAC address.

It's important to see spoofing not as an attack that, by itself, steals data or takes down a service, but as an enabling technique that other attacks build on. A source address that isn't the real one makes it much harder to trace traffic back to its true origin, which is one reason spoofed source addresses show up as a component of certain denial of service techniques, where an attacker wants to hide which machines are actually generating the flood of traffic. It's also a foundational piece of man in the middle attacks, where convincingly impersonating one party's address is often the first step toward inserting an attacker's own machine into a conversation between two others, the subject of the next chapter.

Defending against spoofing generally means not trusting an address field on its own. Networks can filter traffic at their boundary to reject packets whose source address couldn't plausibly have originated from where they entered the network, a technique often called ingress filtering. More broadly, the deeper fix is the same one that runs through this entire chapter: use cryptographic authentication, as in TLS or IPsec, so that trust is based on something an attacker can't simply write into a header, rather than relying on an address field that was never designed to resist forgery in the first place.
